draft.title: The eruption of AD 79
card: Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79. The eruption lasted about two days and buried both Pompeii and Herculaneum.
It lay downwind and was first covered by falling pumice and ash. Roofs collapsed under the weight, but many walls stayed standing.
It was hit by pyroclastic flows, fast clouds of hot gas, ash and rock that rushed down the volcano. They buried the town under many metres of material.

Because the two towns were buried in different ways, they were preserved differently. Herculaneum kept things that rot easily, such as wood and food, while Pompeii kept more of its buildings and their wall paintings.
draft.remember: Falling ash and pumice buried Pompeii. Pyroclastic flows buried Herculaneum. The burial shaped what survived.

opts: Pyroclastic flows of hot gas, ash and rock
Falling pumice and ash over many hours
A tsunami from the Bay of Naples
Lava flows from the crater of Vesuvius
a.why: Herculaneum was buried by pyroclastic flows, which rushed down the volcano and left deep deposits. Falling pumice and ash is what first covered Pompeii, so it is the tempting wrong option.
a.clue: Think about what rushed down the volcano, not what fell from the sky.

b.q: A historian finds a wooden bed and food in a buried Roman town on Vesuvius. Which explanation best fits this find?
opts: Deep pyroclastic flows sealed the town and preserved wood
Falling pumice kept wood safe by leaving the roofs standing
The town was dug up early, so its wood was protected
The town was far from Vesuvius and was only lightly covered
b.why: Deep pyroclastic flows buried Herculaneum and preserved things that rot easily, such as wood and food. Falling pumice at Pompeii collapsed many roofs, so the second option gives the wrong reason.
b.clue: Which burial preserved things that rot easily?

problems.detail: 'Pompeii kept more of its buildings and their wall paintings' is misleading as an effect of burial type. Herculaneum's deep flows often preserved buildings better, including upper storeys, wooden structures and fine wall paintings. Pompeii simply has more of its area excavated.

proposal.title: The eruption of AD 79
card: Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79. The eruption lasted about two days and buried both Pompeii and Herculaneum.
It lay downwind and was first covered by several metres of falling pumice and ash. Many roofs collapsed under the weight.
It lay upwind, so little pumice fell on it. It was hit by pyroclastic flows, fast clouds of hot gas, ash and rock that buried it about 20 metres deep.

The different burials preserved the towns differently. Herculaneum's deep, hot deposit set hard and sealed it, keeping charred wood, food and some upper floors. Pompeii's shallower cover and fallen roofs left fewer upper floors and less wood.
proposal.remember: How each town was buried shaped what survived: deep flows at Herculaneum sealed even wood and food.

opts: Pyroclastic flows of hot gas, ash and rock
Falling pumice and ash over many hours
A tsunami from the Bay of Naples
Lava flows from the crater of Vesuvius
a.why: Herculaneum was buried by pyroclastic flows, which left a deposit about 20 metres deep. Falling pumice and ash is what first covered Pompeii, which lay downwind, so that option describes the wrong town.
a.clue: Which town lay in the path of the falling pumice?

b.q: A historian finds a charred wooden bed and food in a buried Roman town on Vesuvius. Which explanation best fits this find?
opts: Deep pyroclastic flows set hard and sealed the town
Falling pumice kept wood safe by leaving roofs standing
A shallow cover of ash let the wood dry out slowly
Lava flowed over the town and cooled around the wood
b.why: Herculaneum's deep, hot pyroclastic deposit set hard and sealed the town, so wood and food survived as charred remains. The idea that falling pumice left roofs standing is wrong: at Pompeii many roofs collapsed, and less wood survived under its shallower cover.
b.clue: Which kind of burial left the deepest, hardest seal?
